script.speaker: Extract 1
script.text: Extract one. You hear two friends talking about a documentary on urban farming.

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: So, did you end up watching that documentary about rooftop farms? I know you were dying to see it.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: I did, yes. And I have to say, visually it was stunning. The drone shots over Brooklyn alone were worth it. But I came away feeling slightly short-changed, if I'm honest.

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: Really? Everyone at work has been raving about it.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Oh, it's well made, no question. It's just that they kept skating over the economics. You see these gorgeous lettuces, but nobody ever explains who can actually afford to buy them. I'd have liked at least one hard question.

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: That's fair, I suppose. Mind you, I'm not sure a ninety-minute film can do everything. If it gets people thinking about where their food comes from, that's already something.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: I'll give you that. As a conversation starter, it does the job.

script.speaker: Extract 2
script.text: Extract two. You hear a woman talking to a colleague about a conference she has just attended.

script.speaker: Rachel
script.text: I was dreading it, to be honest. Three days of back-to-back presentations in a windowless hotel basement. I'd packed two novels just to survive the evenings.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: And? Did you read them?

script.speaker: Rachel
script.text: Not a single page! What I hadn't bargained for was how much would happen outside the sessions. The talks themselves were pretty uneven, some of them frankly a waste of a slot, but the people I met over coffee have already given me three leads for the new project.

script.speaker: Ben
script.text: So you'd go again next year?

script.speaker: Rachel
script.text: I would, though I'd be far more selective about which sessions I sat through. I'd skip half the programme and treat the corridor as the real conference.

script.speaker: Extract 3
script.text: Extract three. You hear a man talking on a radio programme about taking up the cello as an adult.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: People assume the hardest part of starting an instrument at fifty is physical, that your fingers won't cooperate. Actually, they adapt surprisingly fast. What nearly made me give up was something else entirely: hearing myself. I knew what good playing sounded like, and I was nowhere near it, and that gap was mortifying.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: My teacher's solution was rather clever. She made me record myself every week but forbade me from listening to the recordings for three months. When I finally did, I could hear how far I'd come, rather than how far I still had to go. Now I'd tell any adult beginner: be patient with your ears, not just your hands.

title: Part 2 · Sentence completion: a wildlife sound recordist
instructions: You will hear a sound recordist called Clare Hudson talking about her work. For questions 1-8, complete the sentences with a word or short phrase.

script.speaker: Speaker
script.text: Hi everyone. I'm Clare Hudson, and for the past six years I've worked as a sound recordist for wildlife documentaries. People often imagine my job is mostly about microphones, but honestly, the skill I use most is patience.

script.speaker: Speaker
script.text: I actually trained as a violinist, and I think that's why I notice sounds other people filter out. My first job in the industry wasn't glamorous at all: I spent eight months cataloguing archive recordings of birdsong for a museum in Edinburgh.

script.speaker: Speaker
script.text: The project that changed everything was in the Scottish Highlands, recording red deer during the autumn rut. We'd expected the main challenge to be the cold. In fact, the biggest problem was the wind, which made almost half of our recordings unusable. I ended up building a shield for the microphone out of an old sheepskin rug, and it worked better than the expensive equipment.

script.speaker: Speaker
script.text: People ask whether the sounds in documentaries are real. Mostly, yes, but not always recorded at the same moment as the pictures. Footsteps on snow, for example, are often added later by a team we call Foley artists. My favourite trick is that a bag of cornflour, squeezed slowly, sounds exactly like someone walking through snow.

script.speaker: Speaker
script.text: The most memorable sound I've ever captured was not an animal call at all. It was the sound of ice cracking on a frozen lake in Finland, which sounds almost like a laser in a science-fiction film. Viewers wrote in convinced it had been created artificially.

script.speaker: Speaker
script.text: If you're thinking of getting into this field, my advice is simple. Don't start by buying expensive kit. Start by going outside at dawn with any recorder at all, even a phone, and simply listen for an hour. You'll learn more about sound in that hour than in any course.

title: Part 3 · Interview: the economist who quit his job to make furniture
instructions: You will hear an interview with Marcus Bell, a former economist who now makes furniture. For questions 1-6, choose the answer (A, B, C or D) which fits best according to what you hear.

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: My guest today is Marcus Bell, who spent fifteen years as an economist at a major bank before leaving to become a furniture maker. Marcus, was there a single moment when you decided to go?

script.speaker: Marcus
script.text: Everyone wants there to be one dramatic moment, and journalists have tried very hard to find it. The truth is duller. I didn't hate the job; I was good at it and well paid. It was more that, over several years, I noticed I was only really alive at weekends, when I was in my shed. Eventually the weekdays started to feel like the interruption.

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: How did your colleagues react when you told them?

script.speaker: Marcus
script.text: I'd braced myself for ridicule. One or two did joke about me 'going off to whittle spoons'. But the reaction that stuck with me was envy, quite openly expressed. A senior partner took me aside and said he'd wanted to be a cabinet-maker since he was twelve. That unsettled me more than any criticism could have, because it made me wonder how many people around me were quietly living the wrong life.

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: Your first year was financially very difficult, I believe.

script.speaker: Marcus
script.text: It was. I'd done all the spreadsheets, as you'd expect from an economist, and I'd allowed for a slow start. What I hadn't factored in was how long each piece would take when I was doing it for money rather than pleasure. As a hobbyist, I could spend three weekends on a chair and call it relaxing. Professionally, that's ruinous. I had to learn to be satisfied with 'excellent' rather than 'perfect'.

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: Does your background in economics help you now?

script.speaker: Marcus
script.text: Less than you'd think in the obvious ways. I'm not running regression models on table legs. Where it does help is that I'm not frightened of numbers or of asking clients for proper money. A lot of craftspeople undersell themselves because talking about price feels vulgar to them. I lost that squeamishness years ago, on the trading floor.

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: There's been a lot of talk recently about a craft revival. Do you think it's real?

script.speaker: Marcus
script.text: I'm wary of the word 'revival'. Interest in craft has certainly grown, and that's good for people like me. But much of it is about watching rather than making — people love videos of someone planing wood. Whether that turns into people actually buying handmade things at their true cost, I genuinely don't know. Ask me again in ten years.

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: And finally, would you recommend your path to others?

script.speaker: Marcus
script.text: I'd recommend the question rather than the answer. I wouldn't tell anyone to quit their job; that would be irresponsible. But I'd encourage everyone to notice when they feel most like themselves and to ask whether their life is arranged around that, or around avoiding it.

textOrTranscript:
Interviewer: My guest today is Marcus Bell, who spent fifteen years as an economist at a major bank before leaving to become a furniture maker. Marcus, was there a single moment when you decided to go?

Marcus: Everyone wants there to be one dramatic moment, and journalists have tried very hard to find it. The truth is duller. I didn't hate the job; I was good at it and well paid. It was more that, over several years, I noticed I was only really alive at weekends, when I was in my shed. Eventually the weekdays started to feel like the interruption.

Interviewer: How did your colleagues react when you told them?

Marcus: I'd braced myself for ridicule. One or two did joke about me 'going off to whittle spoons'. But the reaction that stuck with me was envy, quite openly expressed. A senior partner took me aside and said he'd wanted to be a cabinet-maker since he was twelve. That unsettled me more than any criticism could have, because it made me wonder how many people around me were quietly living the wrong life.

Interviewer: Your first year was financially very difficult, I believe.

Marcus: It was. I'd done all the spreadsheets, as you'd expect from an economist, and I'd allowed for a slow start. What I hadn't factored in was how long each piece would take when I was doing it for money rather than pleasure. As a hobbyist, I could spend three weekends on a chair and call it relaxing. Professionally, that's ruinous. I had to learn to be satisfied with 'excellent' rather than 'perfect'.

Interviewer: Does your background in economics help you now?

Marcus: Less than you'd think in the obvious ways. I'm not running regression models on table legs. Where it does help is that I'm not frightened of numbers or of asking clients for proper money. A lot of craftspeople undersell themselves because talking about price feels vulgar to them. I lost that squeamishness years ago, on the trading floor.

Interviewer: There's been a lot of talk recently about a craft revival. Do you think it's real?

Marcus: I'm wary of the word 'revival'. Interest in craft has certainly grown, and that's good for people like me. But much of it is about watching rather than making — people love videos of someone planing wood. Whether that turns into people actually buying handmade things at their true cost, I genuinely don't know. Ask me again in ten years.

Interviewer: And finally, would you recommend your path to others?

Marcus: I'd recommend the question rather than the answer. I wouldn't tell anyone to quit their job; that would be irresponsible. But I'd encourage everyone to notice when they feel most like themselves and to ask whether their life is arranged around that, or around avoiding it.

title: Part 5 · The Myth of the Lone Genius
instructions: You are going to read an article about creativity. For questions 1-6, choose the answer (A, B, C or D) which you think fits best according to the text.
textOrTranscript:
The Myth of the Lone Genius

We like our breakthroughs to come with a face attached. Newton under his apple tree, Edison in his laboratory at three in the morning, a young programmer in a garage: these images are so familiar that they have hardened into a kind of folk theory of creativity. According to this theory, transformative ideas spring from the minds of exceptional individuals working, ideally, against the scepticism of everyone around them. It is a flattering story, both for the geniuses and for the rest of us, who can enjoy their achievements without wondering why we never produce anything similar.

The trouble is that the historical record stubbornly refuses to cooperate. When historians of science look closely at almost any celebrated discovery, they find not a solitary flash of insight but a crowded room. Calculus was developed independently by Newton and Leibniz within a few years of each other; the telephone patent was filed by Alexander Graham Bell on the very day that Elisha Gray submitted a similar design. Such cases are not curiosities. Sociologists have catalogued hundreds of them, and some have gone so far as to argue that 'multiple discovery' is the norm rather than the exception: once the necessary knowledge and tools are in place, an idea is, in a sense, waiting to be found.

This does not mean that individuals are irrelevant. It would be absurd to claim that anyone could have written Hamlet, given the state of English drama in 1600. But it does suggest that we have been asking the wrong question. Instead of 'What made this person a genius?', we might more usefully ask 'What made this environment so fertile?' The answer, more often than not, involves dense networks of people exchanging ideas, competing, borrowing and occasionally stealing from one another.

Consider Renaissance Florence, a city of perhaps 60,000 people that produced, within a couple of generations, a disproportionate share of the most admired art in European history. It is tempting to attribute this to an unusual concentration of talent, as if Florentine mothers had simply given birth to more gifted children. A more plausible explanation lies in the city's peculiar combination of wealthy patrons, fierce rivalry between workshops, and an apprenticeship system that allowed techniques to circulate rapidly. Talent, in other words, was not so much born as manufactured.

None of this has stopped the lone-genius narrative from flourishing, and it is worth asking why. Part of the explanation is simply that stories need protagonists; a biography of a network is a hard book to sell. But there is also something more troubling at work. Organisations that subscribe to the myth tend to reward individual stars at the expense of the collaborative structures that actually generate innovation. Companies poach celebrated researchers at enormous cost, only to discover that their brilliance does not travel well once they are separated from the colleagues and resources that sustained it.

If there is a lesson here, it is not that we should stop admiring remarkable people. It is that admiration, on its own, is a poor guide to policy. Those who want more creativity—in a school, a company or a country—would do better to invest in the unglamorous conditions that make it possible: places where people can meet, time to experiment, and tolerance of the failures that inevitably precede success. The garage, after all, was rarely as empty as the legend suggests.

title: Part 6 · Should homework be abolished?
instructions: You are going to read four extracts in which experts give their views on homework. For questions 1-4, choose from the experts A-D. The experts may be chosen more than once.
textOrTranscript:
Should homework be abolished in secondary schools?

A  Dr Helen Marsh, educational psychologist
The evidence on homework at secondary level is more encouraging than its critics admit. Large-scale studies consistently show a modest but real link between time spent on homework and exam results, particularly for older students. The problem is not homework itself but bad homework: pointless worksheets set out of habit. Abolishing it would penalise precisely those students who lack other opportunities to consolidate what they learn in class. What schools need is not less homework but better-designed tasks, with clear feedback.

B  Mark Adeyemi, head teacher
In my school we scrapped compulsory homework for the first three years of secondary five years ago, and I have no regrets. Exam results did not fall; if anything, they rose slightly, although I would not claim that this was caused by the change. What did change dramatically was the atmosphere: fewer arguments at home, fewer detentions, more students reading for pleasure. I accept that research shows some academic benefit, but I suspect it is too small to justify the stress and family conflict homework creates.

C  Sofia Lindqvist, parent and journalist
Much of the debate ignores the elephant in the room: homework widens inequality. A child with a quiet bedroom, a laptop and educated parents can complete an assignment in an hour. A child sharing a room with two siblings, with no internet access, cannot. Supporters claim homework helps disadvantaged students catch up, but in practice it rewards those who are already advantaged. I am not opposed to independent study, but it should take place in school, where every student has the same resources.

D  Prof. Daniel Cho, education researcher
Both sides tend to overstate their case. The research shows a positive association between homework and achievement in secondary school, but correlation is not causation: motivated students may simply do more homework. What we can say with some confidence is that quality matters far more than quantity. Short, purposeful tasks that students can do without help are the most effective, and they also reduce the inequality problem, since they do not depend on resources at home.

textOrTranscript:
Learning to Read the Sea

When I signed up for a week-long sailing course off the west coast of Scotland, I assumed the hardest part would be the knots. I had practised them for weeks at my kitchen table, tying and untying a length of rope while the kettle boiled. [GAP 1]

Our instructor, a weather-beaten woman called Fiona, spent the first morning not on the boat at all but on the harbour wall, making us stare at the water. 'Tell me what you see,' she kept saying. We saw water. She saw a shift in the wind coming from the north-west, a current running against the tide near the headland, and a patch of darker water that meant a sudden gust was on its way.

[GAP 2] By the third day, I could pick out the ruffled patches that signal a gust, and I had started, without being told, to glance up at the clouds every few minutes.

The real test came on the fourth afternoon, when Fiona announced that she would not be giving any instructions. We were to sail to a small island and back, and she would sit in the stern with her arms folded. [GAP 3]

For the first half hour, things went well. We tacked neatly out of the harbour, and I was even beginning to feel slightly smug. Then the wind dropped almost to nothing, and the four of us began to argue about what to do. One wanted to start the engine; another insisted we wait.

Fiona said nothing until we were back in the harbour. Then she simply nodded at me and said, 'You were looking.' It is the most satisfying compliment I have ever received. [GAP 5]

Since coming home, I have found myself doing the same thing in all sorts of situations: paying attention before acting, noticing small signals rather than charging ahead. [GAP 6] What the course taught me, more than any technical skill, was that most mistakes come not from lack of knowledge but from lack of attention.

title: Part 5 · In Praise of Boredom
instructions: You are going to read an article about boredom. For questions 1-6, choose the answer (A, B, C or D) which you think fits best according to the text.
textOrTranscript:
In Praise of Boredom

For most of human history, boredom was simply part of the furniture of life. Long winter evenings, slow journeys and repetitive work left people with hours in which nothing in particular happened. Today, that emptiness has all but vanished. The moment a queue forms or a train is delayed, a phone appears, and the gap is filled before we have even noticed it was there. It is tempting to see this as an unqualified gain. Why, after all, should anyone want to feel bored?

Psychologists have begun to offer a surprising answer. In a frequently cited experiment, participants were asked to perform a deliberately tedious task, copying numbers from a telephone directory, before being set a test of creative thinking. Compared with a control group who had gone straight to the test, they came up with noticeably more original ideas. The researchers' interpretation was cautious: boredom, they suggested, may not cause creativity so much as clear the ground for it, pushing the mind to wander in search of the stimulation the task has failed to provide.

This idea is not entirely new. Writers and scientists have long reported that their best ideas arrived not at the desk but in the bath, on a walk or while staring out of a window. What is new is the near-total disappearance of such moments. A mind that is never allowed to drift, the argument goes, is a mind that rarely makes the unexpected connections on which original thought depends.

It would be naïve, however, to romanticise boredom. Chronic boredom, the kind experienced by people trapped in monotonous jobs or isolated by circumstance, is associated not with creativity but with depression, risk-taking and poor health. The boredom that seems to be productive is of a particular kind: brief, chosen, and experienced by people who have the freedom to act on whatever ideas it produces. Prescribing more boredom to a factory worker on a twelve-hour shift would be not only useless but insulting.

So what, if anything, should the rest of us do? Some commentators recommend rigid 'digital detox' regimes, but these tend to treat the phone as a kind of addictive substance, to be renounced entirely. A more realistic approach might be to stop treating every empty moment as a problem to be solved. Leaving the phone in a pocket during a ten-minute wait is hardly a heroic act of self-denial. Yet it may be enough to let the mind do something it has been increasingly denied the chance to do: nothing in particular.

Whether this will make anyone more creative is uncertain. The research is still at an early stage, and the effects found in laboratories are often smaller and less reliable in everyday life. But even if the benefits turn out to be modest, there is something to be said for rediscovering a state that our ancestors took for granted, and that we seem to have abolished almost without noticing.

title: Part 7 · The Accidental Beekeeper
instructions: You are going to read an article about beekeeping. Six paragraphs have been removed. Choose from paragraphs A-G the one which fits each gap (1-6). There is one extra paragraph which you do not need to use.
textOrTranscript:
The Accidental Beekeeper

I never intended to keep bees. Three summers ago, a swarm arrived uninvited in the hollow of an old apple tree at the bottom of my garden, and I assumed the sensible thing would be to call someone to take it away. [GAP 1]

Instead, he stood watching the entrance for a long time, then told me that if I left them alone they would probably do perfectly well. He offered to lend me a hive and some basic equipment, 'just in case you change your mind'. I thanked him politely and fully intended to return everything unused.

[GAP 2] By the end of that first summer I was spending my evenings sitting a few metres from the tree, watching the bees come and go and trying to work out what they were carrying on their legs.

The following spring, a neighbour's beekeeper friend helped me transfer the colony into the borrowed hive. It was not a smooth operation. [GAP 3] For a week I was convinced I had killed the whole colony through my own clumsiness.

They survived, of course, and in doing so taught me the first of many lessons in humility. Bees, it turns out, are considerably more resilient than the people who keep them. [GAP 4]

That is not to say that beekeeping is easy. Colonies are vulnerable to disease, to parasites, and to the kind of wet summer that leaves them unable to forage for weeks. [GAP 5] Each loss felt personal, even though experienced beekeepers assured me that it happens to everyone.

What surprises me most, looking back, is how much the bees have changed the way I see the garden. [GAP 6] Now I find myself noticing which flowers are buzzing and which are silent, and choosing plants not for how they look but for what they offer.

title: Part 8 · Learning a language as an adult
instructions: You are going to read four people describing learning a language as an adult. For questions 1-10, choose from the people (A-D). The people may be chosen more than once.
textOrTranscript:
Four people describe learning a language as an adult

A  Marta – Japanese
I started Japanese at forty, mainly because my daughter was studying it and I wanted to understand what she was talking about. I assumed the writing system would be the hardest part, but I actually found it rather soothing, almost like a puzzle. What I really struggled with was speaking: in Japanese, the level of politeness changes depending on who you are talking to, and I was terrified of offending people. A teacher eventually told me that native speakers forgive almost any mistake from a foreigner who is obviously trying, and that freed me to make the mistakes I needed to make.

B  Daniel – Portuguese
I moved to Lisbon for work and expected to pick the language up naturally. I didn't. Everyone at the office spoke English, and after a year I could barely order a coffee. What changed things was joining an amateur football team where nobody spoke English at all. It was humiliating at first; I spent whole matches not understanding instructions. But within six months I was following conversations, and I picked up a lot of slang that no textbook would ever teach you.

C  Fatima – German
I studied German at school decades ago and remembered almost nothing, so I decided to approach it completely differently this time. Instead of grammar exercises, I watched German television series with German subtitles, pausing constantly to look things up. My progress was slow but steady, and I found I remembered words much better when I had heard them in a dramatic scene. My one regret is that I neglected writing; I can follow a complicated conversation, but I still struggle to write a simple email without errors.

D  Kenji – Spanish
I'd always told myself I had no talent for languages, which turned out to be a convenient excuse. When I finally started Spanish, I set myself a strict routine: twenty minutes every morning before work, no exceptions. Some days it felt pointless; I couldn't see any progress at all. But after about eight months something seemed to click, and I suddenly understood far more than I expected. What kept me going through the dull periods was a friend in Mexico whom I spoke to every Sunday.
